I use them instead of reviews a good deal of the time now. I just want to see a game actually being played so I can see if it's something I would enjoy playing. The trick is to find someone who does a good job. TB does great, obviously, and even though we don't share the same tastes he's trustworthy enough to worth watching and if he likes something that goes against his tastes that's enough of a recommendation for me. Metacritic is great for a "bird's eye view" of the review landscape so to speak, but nothing can actually beat seeing the game being played in real time. Words and opinion can try and explain Frozen Synapse, but you have to actually see it in action to really understand it.

For me, Let's Plays are great for seeing what a game is like without installing, booting up, etc. So I'll happily watch ten minutes of pretty much any game I'm thinking about getting. Commentary about the haptic experience is great, and other commentary is fine if it's not distracting. But, this kind of Let's Play is pretty much a commodity unless the game is rare or obscure.

The other reason I'd watch is if the LPer is doing something funny, or pontificating about something really interesting, or showing off a neat trick in the game. Sort of a podcast plus LP. But I can't think of anyone who does this consistently well.

There's maybe one or two exceptions.

Also, shoehorning in your own channel is kinda low. Don't do that. If you want feedback, ask for feedback. Don't try to create a conversation and then force in an advertisement. There are other places you can go for that.

Sandra Bland and the lawful order problem

From the article:

The first problem is knowing what counts as an “order.” If an officer approaches you and asks you to do something, that’s normally just a request and not an order. But if there’s a law on the books saying that you have to comply with the officer’s request, then the request is treated as an order. You can’t know what is an “order” unless you study the law first, which you’re unlikely to have done before the officer approached you.

The even bigger problem is knowing when an order is “lawful.” An order is lawful if forcing compliance would not violate any law. But a citizen is in no position to assess that. Even if the police pulled over the world’s greatest legal expert, the citizen still couldn’t know what orders are lawful because the laws often hinge on facts the citizen can’t know.

The trouble is that, even if you know that a police order is unlawful, the police have all of the force necessary to force compliance - and the will to use it. if the police are later proved to be in error, the individual officers are covered by sovereign immunity and suffer little or no consequences. Consequences belong to the taxpayer.
